Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for
458	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) inquired yesterday as to the issue of old age security cheques prior to Christmas.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall give the answer now.
It is planned to issue these cheques a day or two before the end of the month, just as is the custom in all other months of the year. There are a number of reasons why the decision was made to stick with the usual practice to issue old age security cheques at the end of the month, even in December.
(1)	To issue them at an earlier date would leave a longer than usual gap between pension payments in December and at the end of January. This would undoubtedly prove confusing to numerous pensioners and would cause considerable correspondence.
(2)	Experience has shown that any marked alteration in the date of issue of cheques is followed by a wave of correspondence the next month and by great pressure of telephone calls where our offices are in principal cities, as in Toronto for example. If cheques were issued on the 20th of December, for instance, thousands of pensioners for some reason or other would expect them to be issued on the 20th of January, and so on.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ISSUE OF CHEQUES PRIOR TO CHRISTMAS
speechtext: Why not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ISSUE OF CHEQUES PRIOR TO CHRISTMAS
speechtext:
(3) The mechanical side of the issue of cheques has also to be considered. In all our offices the issue of old age security cheques is closely tied in with the issue of family allowances cheques. It would be most awkward to have to try to get both family allowances cheques and old age security cheques issued by the 20th or 22nd of the month. Our custom is to prepare all family allowances cheques in the first half of the month and the old age security cheques in the latter part of the month. In an office such as Toronto, where more than 600,000 family allowances cheques are prepared, and where about 250,000 old age security cheques are also issued, it is most important to spread the load evenly throughout the month.
(4) Finally, we have been under considerable pressure from the Post Office Department to keep down the volume of mail going out just before Christmas. The issue of nearly 700,000 old age security cheques just before Christmas would add appreciably to the volume of first-class mail and might well mean the loss, misplacement or delay of pension cheques with resulting hardship to pensioners.
On the whole it is felt that the interests of all, pensioners not the least, would be best served by maintaining the usual date of issue at the end of the month. It is the


intention to get the cheques out so that, if at all possible, they will be received just before New Year's day.

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I listened during the past two weeks to hon. members who have participated in this debate I had the feeling that though we represent different political and economic schools of thought and disagree on many subjects there is one thing on which we all agree, that is that we are most fortunate to be living in this favoured land.
We are continually being told of our expanding economy, of our increasing national income and our rising standards of living. To a large extent what is said in that regard is true. Canada is a rich country; there can be no doubt about that. At no time in our history have we been more prosperous than we are today. However, as I see it, there is a fly in the ointment of our prosperity. It may not be a very large fly, but still it is there and it does those things which a fly in the ointment is supposed to do.
Our wealth is not equitably distributed. I have not in mind now a system where everyone gets an even share of the wealth. What I have in mind is the fact that a few of our people have a great deal more than they need, indeed, a great deal more than is good for them. The great mass of our people have enough, as the saying is, to get by on. But a considerable number of our people suffer acutely during a great portion of their lives because of a lack of the very essentials of life.
I do not think that that should be so in a rich country such as this where we have all the means of preventing it. This afternoon I am going to take advantage of the opportunity which this debate offers to draw to the attention of the government and the House of Commons the plight of certain groups among us who are not aware that they are citizens of the richest country on earth. I know that they see the prosperity parade going by but they themselves have no part in it.
The first group I want to mention has been mentioned here many times before. I refer to the recipients of war veterans allowances. In The Legionary for December, a copy of which I presume all hon. members have received, is an article by the editor which ought to be "must" reading for members of the government and indeed for Liberal members generally. It is entitled "The Case for W. V. A. Increases". The writer outlines some of the conditions under which some of those who are in receipt of war veterans allowances exist.
He refers to one Ottawa veteran, a man who enlisted and fought in the first world war, was wounded and gassed, as a result of which he has suffered ill health since

1918. This ill health did not prevent him from working altogether but it did prevent him from holding a job very long. He lost one job after another. His wife is also in poor health. His last job was with the Department of Public Works and he stayed there for quite a long time, for jobs of that kind, nearly ten years.
He and his wife are bringing up a grandson. He applied for and received a war veterans allowance. He is living in what they term a two-room basement suite, but from the conditions described I would call it a cellar, as it is seven feet below the pavement. It was originally used to store coal, which of course was removed before this man and wife and grandchild moved in.
This man is receiving a war veterans allowance of $90 per month and they receive an additional $5 per month as a family allowance for the child. They spend $25 per month on rent, $60 for food, $4 for gas for cooking and $4 for Blue Cross. It will be noted that this man even with his meagre income is making provision for sickness, for doctors' attendance and hospitalization. Then he pays $2.36 for insurance, making a total of $95.36 or 36 cents more than his total income.
The writer in The Legionary points out that this does not leave room for things such as books, a radio, clothing, china, replacement of furniture and the hundred and one things that most of us consider absolute essentials of present-day life.
Perhaps it would not be fair to say that this case is typical, but it is not an isolated case. It indicates quite clearly that the war veterans allowance at the present time is not adequate. The article refers to a survey which the Legion carried out across Canada, and states:
In case after case, food and rent devour three quarters of their budgets. In a dozen cases, they report they are living in shacks, others in cabins or in cottages. They live in single rooms, in homes that frequently need repair, live with relatives and friends. One totally disabled veteran lives with his wife and three children in three basement rooms.
And so on. Over a period of time the Legion has made representations to the government and to the veterans committee that dealt with this matter. I believe that they are asking for $60 a month for single veterans and $120 a month for married veterans. I think any hon. member of this house who will consider the present cost of living is bound to say that the Legion is most modest in the demands that it makes, that no single man could live decently today on $50 a month, nor could any married man and his wife live

4G1

decently on $90 a month. I say it is a disgrace to us who live in Canada, a country as richly endowed as ours, that these things should exist.
There is another still smaller group to which I wish to refer. I have in mind those receiving the blind persons' allowance. I am not going to say very much about them. If my memory serves me right, there are only about 12,000 in Canada altogether, but I believe they are entitled to our particular consideration because of their infirmity. They are entitled to more thought and sympathy than we would perhaps give to less handicapped people. I think I can put the case best as I see it by reading from an article that appeared in the Vancouver Province on April 14 of this year. The author is Mr. D. A. McGregor. I do not know whether he is a columnist or one of the editors of the paper. He has this to say:
If an ordinary individual has an income of $1,000 or less, he is not required to pay any income tax. The assumption is that he isn't financially able to do so. But if a blind person on a pension dares, by his own efforts, to push his income beyond $840 the same compassionate law which awards him the pension will take everything beyond $840 away.
That is the way it is, and put that way it is most striking. Then he goes on to deal with the married blind person as follows:
The Income Tax Act assumes a married couple need $2,000 a year. But if the married blind pensioner, or his wife, adds more than $360 to the pension, and brings the family income over $1,320 he too will have the excess deducted. The money is not taxed away, but it is lifted from the pensioner's purse as effectively as if it were.
So far as those on the blind persons allowance and those on war veterans allowance are concerned, I say that we should remove at once the limit on their outside income. Why in the world should a person on war veterans allowance be restricted to earning not more than $10 a month? You know, that is not only bad for that person but it is bad for everyone. Work is good for a man. It adds to his self-respect and selfesteem. It makes him a better citizen, and I cannot see who would be hurt if we allowed a person receiving the war veterans allowance to earn $50 a month. No one would be hurt and everyone would be better off including, I am sure, the government because the standard of citizenship in this country would be improved.
There is one class comprising quite a number of people, although not very large, with which I wish to deal. I refer to the superannuated federal civil servants who are living on a very small income which they put aside with the assistance of the government at a time when the amount of the pension they now receive meant a great
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis deal more than it does today. I do not believe we should say that we have no responsibility for these people. After all, they are citizens of Canada who gave service to Canada during the years when they were able to give service, and if what they put aside during those years is not sufficient today to provide anything like a decent standard of living that is not their fault. If there is fault then it is our collective fault, and collectively we should remedy it by making further provision for them.
The number of people involved and the amounts they receive have been put on the record so often by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that perhaps I should not take the time of the house today to repeat this information. However, I will put some figures on the record and those I wish to quote are as of March, 1952. There are 1,106 receiving less than $20 per month. From $20 to $29.99-let us say $30 because it is simpler-there are 1,365. From $30 to $40 there are 1,417. From $50 to $60 there are 1,384 and from $60 to $70 there are 1,017. There are approximately another 4,000 who receive from $80 to $100. All these people, and particularly where there are dependents involved, are not receiving sufficient income-and I say again through no fault of their own-to be able to provide themselves and their dependents with a decent standard of living. During this session of parliament, while our economy is booming, is the time to take action in all the cases I have mentioned, and I hope that those responsible will remedy these defects and enable these people to partake of the prosperity which is a part of the life of most citizens of Canada.
I now wish to say a few words with respect to the amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) which urges that at this session of parliament a measure be introduced to provide for national health insurance. In listening to the speeches and the references to this matter I have found that there is very little opposition in the house to such a program. There has been a little double talk but as far as I have been able to see there is no general opposition. I believe there was one speaker who opposed national health insurance. Today it is something that is accepted in every civilized country as an essential part of their social security legislation. Some members said they were going to vote against the C.C.F. amendment because it proposed state medicine.
Really, I don't know what state medicine is. No one has told me during this debate, but, if they have read that into the amendment, they have read a great deal more into
462	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Maclnnis 'the amendment than is in it. After ail, what does the amendment do? It does not outline any system of health insurance. It asks this government at this session to introduce a measure for national health insurance. What that measure would be would depend on the kind of legislation this government would introduce.
May I just say in passing that I have been in this house for some considerable time and, looking at these matters objectively, I am sure that this group would give its support to any measure-no matter what we considered or thought of it ourselves, and whether we thought it was what we would do or not, but we would support any measure that we considered to be in the interests of the people of Canada. We would consider it on its merits and we would not boggle at whether there was this in it or that in it if we felt it would serve the people of this country. Those who say that they are opposed to the amendment because the C.C.F. wants state medicine are just talking through their hats.
The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair)- and I may say here that there is no man in this house for whom I have greater respect- got himself all balled up over this question, largely, in my opinion, because the hon. gentleman is himself in favour of national health insurance, though he is not quite sure that the party to which he belongs is in favour of national health insurance. In the course of his speech, the written and the oral one, he lias made two or three proposals and concludes by saying that he is opposed to the C.C.F. amendment and is going to vote against it because it is state medicine. I just suggest to him that whether it is his party or the party now in power that brings in a national health insurance measure-as I said before, whether it completely agrees with what we have in mind or not-if it will serve the people of Canada we will support it.
By the way. the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) said that he too was opposed to state medicine and I noticed that when he said that he looked towards this group. I think that what differentiates so-called state medicine from ordinary health insurance, or what my friends would consider satisfactory health insurance, is the question of whether doctors are on salary or on a fee-for-service basis.

The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) says that it was compulsory under the former government. If the present government is not going to make it compulsory, I suggest to them they make it noncompulsory for the employee as well as for the other fellow.
This note says:
Your enclosed billing is more than a bill which should be paid: it is your peace of mind in the event that you may have to go to hospital; it is your protection against high hospital bills which could ruin your finances;
I know some finances which it would not take much to ruin.
It ensures that the best hospital care is available; it provides the best answer to the problem of acute hospital care and accommodation.
In short, when you pay this bill, you are investing, at less than 11 cents a day, in your most precious possessions-good health and freedom from hospital bills.
I do not think that any government should be ashamed to make a thing like that compulsory. I believe a government that does not make it compulsory is delinquent in its duties.
There is another item I want to read, merely to show the general opinion in my province in regard to health insurance of which, as I said before, this is a very essential part. I have here an editorial from the Nelson News, and I regret that I did not put a date on it. I believe it appeared about two days before the provincial election, which would be about June 10, 1952. The editorial reads:
Hospital insurance service is giving hospitalization to those who need it probably as cheaply as it is possible to do so. This is a fact easily recognized by those who have had to foot hospital, X-ray, therapeutic or laboratory services and drug bills in the past. Moreover, because it is supported chiefly by direct payments we know what it is costing, avoiding the necessity of additional hidden taxes.
The service and coverage has its faults. But the introduction of any scheme of its scope is likely to initial hesitancies and errors. There is no need to excuse them, but sensible people who have something good can always correct faults to make it better. In the meantime,-
This is what I want the members of this house to notice.
-during the 3l -year history of the hospital insurance scheme over 740,000 patients have found their hospital bills relatively trifling because of this social legislation.
I was unfortunate enough to be one of those 740,000 patients, but fortunate that I had the benefit of the hospital insurance service. I

The Address-Mr. Maclnnis would hate to tell this house what it cost on my behalf. When we propose, as we have proposed, that a measure be brought in to this house to make this complete, we appreciate it is a matter of dominion-provincial cooperation. When the federal government initiated other social services, we did not always wait until all the provinces were ready. In the case of old age pensions, for instance, some of the provinces were not ready for many years. I believe the only province that was ready when the legislation became law was the province of British Columbia. That province had legislation passed and was ready to take advantage of the federal enactment as soon as it became law. From 1927 until the last province came in about 1936, if my memory serves me correctly, there was a nine-year period before some of the other provinces were ready. But that is no reason why those provinces that are willing to proceed with national health insurance should not be given an opportunity. It is extremely democratic. It is legislation by consent, and no one need be ashamed of proposing it; certainly, we are not.
There was one other matter to which I wished to refer, and I hope I may have time to say a few words about it because I believe that, as the days go by, it will become more and more important. I was interested in the statement made by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) when he spoke in this debate on December 1. He was asked the following question by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), as it appears at page 236 of Hansard for that date:

Perhaps for you, but not for me. I continue the quotation:
-but I would say that the greatest welfare that can come to the people is to leave with them their absolute freedom to act according to their own conscience and will, and see that their incomes are such that they can make available to themselves the highest standard of living the resources of the country can give without interfering with that freedom. That to me is the greatest possible welfare state.
If that means anything at all, it means that what our Social Credit friends have in mind is that enough money will be made available to every person to do whatever he wants to do. I am not opposed to that if such a thing could be done. But after all,


that must mean one of two things. It must mean that there is an unlimited pool, trunk or bank of money into which everyone can dip ad lib and take whatever he wants, or it has to be'given out by somebody. If it is the first-well, all they have to do is to dip. But if the second-and I should like to hear some explanation of this-someone has to decide how much each one will get.
Now, while I am on the subject, there is another thing that I have asked on various occasions when I have been on the platform with Social Crediters. A fundamental part of the Social Credit system is the just price and the national dividend. What I want to know first of all is, who is going to set the just price? Can the just price be set without government interference? Somebody has to set it. Who is to say what the size of the dividend will be? These questions are important, because in my opinion, the people are being deluded with certain economic proposals, mixing them up with reference to the "eternal verities", whatever that may be. But some day, if the people are not wise, they will be confronted with a situation they did not foresee, and instead of having a bank of money into which they can dip ad lib, they will have chaos.

am sorry, but I am following an hon. member for whom I have the greatest respect, and I think everybody in the house has. He is one of the oldest members-I mean in years of service-here, and I can assure you that in my province he is highly thought of by all parties. In my own riding he is welcome at any time, and I should be glad to introduce him. That is more than I can say of some. In my riding we respect anybody who is sincere. For sectional hypocrites I have no respect, and I have no desire to have them in my riding.
First of all, I want to congratulate the government, because so far congratulations have been going the other way. I want to congratulate the government on their appointing two cabinet ministers from the province of British Columbia. I do not think anybody disputes the fact that we are the fastest growing province in Canada. I do not, say we are the best province-I will attend to that later-but we are the fastest growing of any province of Canada. We thought long ago that we were entitled to two ministers. Fortunately, at this time, two men were available of such high calibre. I can assure the house that each and every Liberal member in the province of British Columbia is proud of these two cabinet ministers, and will work in perfect harmony with them.
I intend to get right down to health insurance, seeing that my friend has got

into it. I think we had better say what health insurance is. Every member on this side of the house is in favour of health insurance. I can well remember that some years ago, believe it or not, I tried to have adopted some of the legislation that they had in Saskatchewan or perhaps Alberta. I refer to the municipal health insurance plan. I tried to get the municipal act amended in British Columbia so that we could put it in. I ran into my first experience with lobbying at the Empress hotel. Ninety-eight per cent of the doctors of Vancouver were over there to see that I did not get the amendment to the legislation. They did that by lobbying. I have come to the conclusion that probably they were right and I was wrong at that time.
We were criticized outside the house when we brought in family allowances, and particularly by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) who did his utmost to defeat it. I presume he had the entire support of his party. They said that we brought it in at a certain date for political purposes. If you will remember, Mr. Speaker, although the legislation was brought down, it did not go into effect at once. If my memory serves me correctly it did not come into effect until July. They said that it was an election dodge. The reason it was not brought in immediately it was passed was that they had to perfect an organization for administration, and so on. The result was that when family allowances were first paid they were paid without a hitch.
You will remember another piece of legislation we brought in, namely, unemployment insurance. We did not put that into effect the date we passed it in this house, or that month, because we had to perfect an organization to carry unemployment insurance into effect without any hitches. I ask you, I ask any labour man, if it has not been administered in that way? The reason I mentioned that is this: I am sorry to say that in British Columbia we had a government that had some Liberals in it. I will not say they were Liberals, but they thought they were. They brought in a hospital insurance scheme. Ninety-five per cent of the people of the province of British Columbia were and are in favour of hospital insurance; but at least 95 per cent also were not in favour of maternity wards being placed in corridors.
I know very little about maternity wards, but I know something about hospitals. I have not had any experience with maternity wards except to watch expectant fathers gaze through glass partitions, but I know a corridor of a hospital is not the proper place for one. What I am getting at is this. I
The Address-Mr. Cruickshank believe that every hon. member on this side of the house would be just as much in favour of hospital insurance as are our good friends of the C.C.F. party. But we believe it must be brought in in an orderly manner. We brought hospital insurance into effect in the province of British Columbia in a half-baked way through overzeal and high pressure. A clerk from the Public Works Department was put in charge of it to begin with, instead of bringing in somebody qualified, perhaps from one of the big corporations, insurance or otherwise. The result was that our hospital insurance in British Columbia was a farce. The intent was there; the intent was good. Perhaps the premier was not careful enough. I think we had three different assessments in one year. We did not have the system organized. We do know that at Christmas time-I think it was about a year ago- people could not get into the hospital; they could not even get into the corridors of the hospitals in the province of British Columbia.
A new outfit came along. I was going to say a new government came along, but, Mr. Speaker, even I cannot use flattering language when it is not deserved. This temporary organization moved into Victoria and they said: "We are going to make it noncompulsory." We happened to be at Ottawa when they came out with this story. I understand that a few members elected to the federal house to represent their federal ridings were not here in Ottawa, but were out there campaigning. They were going around on the hustings saying that they were going to make it non-compulsory. I ask any hon. member in this house-and I believe that 261 of them have common sense-how you can make a hospital insurance scheme non-compulsory. Is it reasonable to expect Jones to pay when Smith does not? I wonder whether the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) thinks he will collect his income tax on a voluntary basis? Will the city of Ottawa collect its municipal taxes on a voluntary basis? No. It was a good hoax to get the people to vote; that is all it was. But it did not work. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) read the little document that you get with your bill now. They have found it would not work and that it was not common sense. Why should I waste so much of my time talking about a non-existent government in British Columbia? But I do want to make it clear that at least I am, as I think every member on this side of the house is, in favour of health insurance, but we do not believe that we are in a position to put it into effect. In my opinion, what we should do is this-and I shall just quote you one possible scheme about to be put into effect in my own riding.

The Address-Mr. Cruickshank A minimum amount of $800,000 is being secured to construct a new fifty-bed hospital. As I understand it, the federal government gives $1,000 a bed now. I think we should double that, and double it immediately, for the construction of new hospitals and hospital accommodation. I believe we should give scholarships to provide more doctors and more dentists. If we had all the hospital beds we needed today, we have not the doctors and dentists in Canada that would be required to provide a health insurance scheme. I believe this government should double whatever we are giving at the present time to construct new hospitals and to provide scholarships or some other means so that we may have more doctors and dentists and nurses.
Then, I think the government has fallen down, and that we as members of parliament have fallen down in another respect. This year out west we had a serious polio epidemic. There was one in eastern Canada too, but I understand it was worse in the west. To my mind it is a disgrace to know that a country like this found it necessary to improvise in the matter of iron lungs. I am not sure how they operate, but I do know that we had to improvise, and fly them in. I say that at this session, as one of the first steps in health insurance, parliament should provide an iron lung to each hospital in Canada that has the facilities to use it.
There is one point that has not been stressed by my hon. friends in the C.C.F., and that is that there should be no hospital in the country in which the poorest patient should not be permitted to have exactly the same medical treatment as the richest patient. It is a disgrace in a country like Canada that at the time of a polio epidemic we have had to improvise in the matter of iron lungs, and fly them in from other parts of Canada or from the United States. At this session we should arrange to see that each hospital in this country that has the facilities should have as many as it needs. I believe we should double our grants to hospitals for new beds.
I find it difficult to speak about war veterans, because this subject has been so well covered by several other speakers in the debate, both on this side and the other side of the house. Since coming to Ottawa I have had the privilege of serving on the war veterans committee. I hope one will be set up this year and that I may serve on it again. I would hope, too, that it might be made a permanent committee.
I wish to support wholeheartedly what has been said by the Canadian Legion in connection with war veterans. I do not think


that a country as wealthy as this one has done what it should have done for our bumt-out veterans. Newspaper articles have been quoted, and perhaps I might be permitted to quote briefly from the Vancouver Sun. I do so because I fear that too many of my colleagues in the House of Commons, possibly because they are not veterans, lose sight of the fact that the war veterans allowance was first brought in to care for those who, through their service in France in the first great war, were pre-aged. The estimate given at that time was ten years. I am speaking about the veterans of the first war, because I do not know about the second one. I do have knowledge of the first great war because I was there. Anyone who served then in France was pre-aged by at least ten years, and this regulation was brought in to cover that pre-ageing. The editorial to which I am referring, and which is headed "They Deserve Better", states:
But as the Legion puts it, the whole concept of WVA was based on recognition that the nation owes a special debt to men who sacrificed health and years of their lives to their country in overseas service. It's not comparable with similar awards to civilians.
I was one who for many years, even before I came to the House of Commons, worked for old age pensions. I am sure any recipient of that pension will agree that a veteran of similar age is entitled to different recognition. If, in other words, the old age pensioner is to receive his payment at the age of 65, then surely the veteran should receive his at the age of 60. To me that seems reasonable, and I suggest the government should take action at this present session in that matter. I would prefer to see a committee set up; but even if it is not, it would be a simple matter to amend the legislation. And if it were done I do not believe the final cost would be much more than it now costs to have the gestapo floating around the country and prying into the lives of men and women who gave so much for us, and whose ability is impaired. But, even if it is not, they are not allowed to earn any substantial sum of money, owing to the fool regulations now in existence. It would not cost as much to treat those people properly as it does to have the gestapo running around.
I wish now to speak about a matter which concerns particularly my own riding, but I believe also concerns the whole of British Columbia as well. I refer to river bank erosion. One of my colleagues from Quebec has on the order paper a resolution dealing with this subject, and referring particularly to the St. Lawrence river. Nothing is of greater concern to the Fraser valley or to the

economy of British Columbia than river bank erosion. It is serious enough when any municipality in the Fraser valley is flooded out, but it is a much more serious thing if, as happened in 1948, the third largest city in Canada is cut off from the rest of the country for a month or two. Particularly is it important to the rest of Canada that that third city, our Pacific port, the outlet to Korea and other eastern ports, should not be cut off during a time of war.
I wish to point out to the government how serious this matter it. It is not enough to say that this is a matter of local concern. Anyone who knows anything about river bank erosion or flooding knows that local districts cannot afford to pay to avoid it, and that they should not be asked to when they are protecting the economy of the whole country. One of the reasons our floods are more frequent now is that our country has been logged over.
There is a paragraph in the speech from the throne which, through the co-operation of federal, provincial and municipal authorities, would afford some relief. I believe this problem could be handled under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. There is no reason why it should not be effective in every province, and it should not be restricted only to two or three provinces. That act should cover every province in Canada, and I would hope that the government might take this fact into consideration at the present session.
I wish to speak briefly about another subject. I do not want to deal with it at length, because I have been a lone wolf for too long in the matter. I refer to the subject of margarine. Today I am not going to worry about margarine as margarine. I will admit it is here to stay, except in two provinces.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the mover (Mr. Deslieres) and the seconder (Mr. Schneider) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, with special reference to the remarks by the seconder about the blind. I should like to add my voice to his in urging the government to give greater consideration to these seriously handicapped persons. The blind associations for years pressed to have blind pensions separated from old age pensions and brought under a separate act. They asked also that the description be changed from blind pension to blindness allowance. This was provided for when the Old Age Security Act was passed along with the separate Blind Persons Act.
I am informed that a few blind persons have discovered that they are actually receiving less under the new legislation than they received before. I am sure that when these acts were passed no one envisaged such a situation arising. I understand this is brought about by the provincial grants for which they are eligible. I would hope that the department concerned will take up this matter and if necessary introduce an amendment to the Blind Persons Act so that no blind person will be in the position where he is actually receiving less than he was before the act was passed.
I should like also to urge the government to remove the means test from the blindness allowance. There are far more reasons for doing this than there were for removing the means test in the case of the old age pensions. It is an anachronism that the means test for the blind should be retained when it has been removed at age 70 as far as old age pensioners are concerned. All the arguments we have heard for years for the removal of the means test in the case of the old age pensions apply equally to the blindness allowance. It kills initiative. It discourages many blind people from going out and earning a little

money, and particularly the cost of administration must represent a considerable proportion of any amount which is saved to the taxpayers by the maintenance of the means test.
The total cost of removing the means test would be quite small and I would hope that in the forthcoming budget it will be provided that this means test be done away with. As a matter of fact, some time ago I saw a newspaper account which reported that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) had held out some hope that this action might be taken. I certainly hope that that report is correct.
There is one other matter in connection with the blind. I remember that the late Arthur Smith, my colleague from Calgary West, urged at practically every session he was here that a greater pension should be paid to the blind and particularly that the age limit in connection with the blindness allowance should be lowered. He could never see, and neither could I, why a blind person should only receive the allowance on reaching the age of 21. I would think that the age could very well be lowered to at least 16 when family allowance payments cease. Certainly the parents of a blind child have considerably greater expenses in bringing up that child than do the parents of a sighted child, and it seems to me that, the parents having carried the full burden up to the age of 16, at which time the family allowance ceases, blind persons should then be given the blindness allowance.
I should now like to touch briefly on certain matters which are of great concern to our most important industry in Canada, agriculture. In my own province of Alberta, in spite of the fact that world attention has been focused on that area because of the great discoveries of gas and oil in the past few years, it remains a fact that the great majority of the people are dependent for their living, either directly or indirectly, upon agriculture.
This year in western Canada we had in aggravated form the difficulty experienced for some time past in getting the grain delivered to the elevators and moved to an export position. Shortly before I came down here I talked to a number of farmers who had large amounts of grain on their farms in granaries and in open piles in fields because they were unable to deliver it to the elevators. One man, whose story I shall give as an example, grew a very large crop of oats this year. He happens to be in a coarse grain growing area, and his yield was better than 100 bushels to the acre. He was allowed to deliver 6 bushels to the acre, I believe, which brought him a cash advance
The Address-Mr. Harkness of about $3 per acre. His expenses for harvesting the oats had been $1 an acre for swathing and $4 an acre for combining, or a total of $5 an acre. All the money he got back, and as far as he could see all he was going to get back for some time, was $3 an acre which left him in the position where he was not able to pay his harvesting expenses, his store bills and so on.
The situation is worse this year than ever before because the largest crop on record was harvested this fall. We had good weather for harvesting and the crop was all brought in. None of it had to be left in the fields over the winter. In addition, the situation is bad because at the time that the new crop began to be ready the elevators and the entire handling system were clogged by the poor quality crop harvested last year. The government is responsible for this condition to a very large extent because the policy they followed was one which made it impossible to dispose of the large amount of low quality wheat delivered to the elevators last year and this spring. That wheat was No. 6 and feed wheat which is unfit for milling purposes and must be used for livestock feed and things of that kind.
Feed wheat was held at a price of $1.50 a bushel and at that price no one feeding livestock would buy it who had experimented with it and knew the situation, when at the same time No. 1 feed barley was available at $1.20 to $1.30 a bushel. There is a great deal more feed value in a bushel of No. 1 feed barley than in a bushel of feed wheat. The result was that a large amount of such wheat remained on hand clogging the handling facilities.
The general situation is that the handling method we have now is out of date. It was built up during a period when harvesting was carried on by binders and wheat was delivered from the farms to elevators by teams and wagons during the course of the winter. Therefore the rate of delivery of the grain was spread out and was gradual. Harvesting methods have changed. The crop in a given year is now taken off very rapidly. It is hauled immediately to elevators by means of trucks, and the present handling facilities are not capable of dealing with it.
Unfortunately, however, nothing has been done to improve the situation. The difficulty in delivering grain is going to continue until some remedy is found, and a remedy must be found. It is not a situation that we can let go on indefinitely. The government has done absolutely nothing with respect to the matter and is to be censured for its inaction. Some farm organizations have suggested that a system of storage of grain on the farms

The Address-^Mr. Harkness combined with cash advances for grain so stored should be instituted by the wheat board. This may be the solution. I do not know because I am not sufficiently expert on these things to be able to tell.
However, I am quite certain that there are solutions to the problem, but the government is not going to find them by following its present course. It has shirked its responsibility completely. It has done nothing, and as a result western farmers have been left holding the bag so far as getting a return for their grain is concerned.
I should like to turn now to the livestock industry. Everyone engaged in that industry knows that things have not been good for most of the past year. The foot-and-mouth outbreak cut off our one remaining market for livestock outside Canada. Fortunately it was announced a short time ago that the United States ban on imports to that country will be lifted on March 1 next, and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that when this announcement was made a great load of anxiety was also lifted from cattle producers right across the country. When we come to hogs the present situation can only be described as disastrous; and when the drop in floor price of $3 per hundred comes into effect on January 1, as announced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), the hog situation will be absolutely impossible. A little over a year ago, on January 15, 1951, I put on the record here a breakdown of the cost of raising hogs, showing that the feed cost alone to bring a pig to market in Ontario at that time was $39. Since then the price of grain has gone up and I would estimate that the cost at the present time for feed alone to produce a 200 pound pig is $41. The price paid for the best pigs, A grade, is $26 per hundredweight in Toronto and Montreal. The return to the farmer on a 200 pound pig which dresses 155 pounds-really a little above average-is $40.30. To this must be added the $2 premium which is paid by the dominion government for the production of high quality bacon. So the farmer receives $42.30 for his pig-$1.30 more than the cost of his feed alone. Out of that $1.30 he has to pay the cost of transporting the pig to market. He has to pay condemnation insurance and in many cases he has to pay commission. So you can take it, generally speaking, that for every A grade pig a farmer produces it has cost him for feed alone as much as he receives for the pig-feed which he had to buy or, if he produced it himself, he could have sold for that figure.

In many cases they have cut down production and are holding on waiting for the day when present conditions will bring about a scarcity and prices will shoot away up-a thing which of course a large number of farmers cannot afford to do.
Now, it would appear to be the deliberate policy of this government to destroy the hog industry in Canada. This appears clearly enough if the support prices which are offered for hogs are compared with the support prices offered for cattle. As of January 1 the support price for each will be $23 per hundred weight, but in the case of hogs this $23 will be for 100 pounds of warm dressed meat. In the case of cattle it is $23 per 100 pounds, live weight. If you work out the support price for cattle on the-same basis as for hogs, that is on a dressed weight basis, it gives you $41 per hundred. Dressed weight is, on the average, 55 per cent of the live weight. You have a differential in the support prices-$23 for hogs as against $41 for cattle.
Now, that is clearly a case of gross discrimination against the hog producer-a deliberate attempt, I would say, to drive the hog producers out of the market. It appears particularly so when you look at the longterm average of the price of hogs as compared with the price of cattle. Now, the reason that they are doing this is not very difficult to guess. For a long time the market for our surplus hogs has been in Great Britain. The hog industry of this country was deliberately built up over many years by means of dominion government subsidies, by importing certain types of boars and by various devices, in order to meet the requirements of this British market. The market has been lost as a result of the policies pursued by this government, and in order to avoid the consequent problems the government is destroying the hog industry without any consideration for the people who have earned their livelihood from it and who are going to suffer serious losses as a result of government policy.
However, more important than the losses suffered by individuals at the present time is the long-term effect of this policy. It will be very serious. In the first place, destruction of the hog industry in this country is going to remove the principal market for coarse grains and low-grade wheat. We come right back to the point with which I started: the large surplus of low-grade wheat which is cluttering up our elevators and our distribution system at the present time. The eventual result, of course, will be the extreme scarcity of hogs, and consequently the consumer will be paying a much higher price than he would otherwise be required to pay.
Another branch of agriculture which is important in Alberta, and upon which I should like to touch very briefly, is the sugar beet industry. The policy which has been followed by the government in regard to this crop is placing it in a precarious situation. Sugar beets are the basis of successful irrigation farming in southern Alberta. The building of the St. Mary dam and the canals leading from it to distribute the water so stored, a project about which we have talked frequently in this house over the past several years, is now more or less completed. In order to make the large expenditure on this project worth while, it is essential to keep the sugar beet industry in a healthy state. The irrigated lands in southern Alberta have been responsible for a very large increase in population. There will be a further increase as a result of this new dry land being brought under irrigation.

In the event of a war, the importance of a domestic supply of sugar is quite apparent. We all know that rationing of sugar took place during both wars, and actually an assured supply of sugar is just as important a defence requirement as any other, because our outside sources of supply may be cut off. This industry is being threatened by what I believe was a mistake made by the government. I was going to say "a pure mistake", but there cannot be such a thing as a pure mistake. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), through an understandable desire to increase our external trade, and one with which I thoroughly agree, made an arrangement with Cuba by which it was hoped a certain amount of Canadian goods, particularly dried codfish and potatoes, would be shipped to Cuba in exchange for 75,000 tons of raw sugar per year. I have no objection to that arrangement. The only trouble is that no means was provided to prevent an unrestricted flow of Cuban refined sugar into Canada.
Cuba now has a large surplus of sugar which she is extremely anxious to dispose of. All the sugar beet industry is asking for is that a quota of some sort be imposed on the importation of refined sugar. They are not asking for a tariff or anything of that sort. All they want is an assurance that the Canadian market is not flooded with this great surplus of Cuban sugar, resulting in the destruction of their industry. This industry might be destroyed in the course of a year or two, by which time the surplus sugar would be gone. A short crop in the cane producing areas might leave the world position such that the price would go to great heights. It seems to me reasonable that these people should be given some consideration in this matter. As someone said to me, it is very desirable to increase our foreign trade with Cuba and other countries, but it seems stupid to buy a Cadillac in order to sell a bag of potatoes, and that is essentially what this sort of deal means.

In the few minutes I have left, I should like to turn to defence matters. Evidently defence is a very touchy subject with the Liberal members, because during the course of this debate so many of them have attempted to explain away the instances of extravagance and waste which have been brought to the attention of the house. In his speech on this matter the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) attempted to use some remark that I made in 1949 as an endorsation of the course which the government has been following. It is extremely flattering that the minister should spend so much time in looking up what one said back in 1949, particularly since the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said that the Minister of National Defence was so busy he did not have time to scrutinize defence contracts. In view of what the minister said about ghost writers, no one would for a moment suggest that he had not looked up these references himself and prepared his speech himself. From his own words, we can only take it that is the situation. It is rather surprising to me that he should have spent so much time looking over these old Hansards to find instances of this sort.
The main thing is, however, that the statement ascribed to me-which of course I made-is not really applicable to what the minister has been doing and what has been done generally by the Department of Defence Production. The quotation the minister used is found on page 135 of Hansard for November 27, and was a reference to what I had said in regard to the difficulty of equipping troops in 1939. I went on to say that there should not be any repetition of that; there is no need for it, particularly with the large amount spent for defence purposes at the present time. I interjected that there was no need to go to extremes, either, and the minister said:
I am glad to see that the hon. member is here and he will no doubt support what he said in 1949.
Certainly I support it, Mr. Speaker, and I support it one hundred per cent. As I say, however, it is not applicable to what the government has been doing so far as our so-called rearmament program is concerned. To begin with, of course, there has to be reason in all things. The provision of a proper quantity of mobilization stores of any sort does not mean the provision of many times the amount that is likely to be required. No one in Canada argues that we should not have adequate supplies of mobilization stores. Actually what has been done has been the buying of large quantities of things which are not essential for mobilization, and at the same time the failure to provide things
The Address-Mr. Harkness which are essential for mobilization. Great quantities of neckties, carpets, teapots, furniture, boudoir lamps and so forth have been secured, but at the same time stocks of rifles, machine guns and artillery pieces have actually been depleted. In other words, during the past two years of heavy expenditures for rearmament the essential mobilization stores have not been stockpiled, and stockpiling is given by the government as the reason expenditures have had to be so great.
For example, we have sent to European countries the arms and equipment for three infantry divisions, plus field pieces for at least one regiment, and I believe practically all the self-propelled anti-tank guns we had. One may well ask the question, then, what has been secured to replace them? Well, if we look at the information supplied to the defence expenditures committee last year, particularly in an exhibit having to do with Canadian defence orders, April 1950 to January 1952, we see at page 16 that we have secured 138 105-millimeter howitzers. These are field pieces to replace the 25-pounder gun-howitzers which were sent to Europe. The number sent to Europe would be 240 25-pounders. Therefore the number we have secured subtracted from that number leaves us with a deficiency of 102 field guns. We are that many field guns worse off than we were before rearmament started.
When we come to rifles I think it is perhaps conservative to say that the equipment for the three divisions included at least 30,000 rifles. To replace them we have ordered, as shown on page 11 of the same exhibit, 12,250 rifles and 7,481 carbines, which apparently take the place of rifles, as it was explained to us. That is 19,000 odd, just under two-thirds as many as were disposed of.
The same story runs through a good deal of the actual fighting equipment which we had at the end of the war and which we have been supposedly ordering since. Some of it we have not only not stockpiled, but we have depleted the stockpiles we had at the end of the war. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in the excitement that has been engendered by the disclosure of the large number of non-essential items which were secured, the serious deficiencies in essential items of fighting equipment have been lost sight of by the general public, or perhaps have never made a real impact on the consciousness of the country as a whole.
There is, of course, a good reason why this should be so, and that is the fact that security is always invoked as a reason for

The opposition have been repeating old accusations, have been hurling old charges which have been answered time and again. We heard them referring time after time to waste and extravagance in the Department of National Defence and the Department of Defence Production. Those accusations were brought before the committee that was set up last year and satisfactory evidence was given. I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey) for the speech he made the other day on this subject. He showed that most of these accusations had been answered. He showed that information had been given by officers of the department at the hearings of the committee, and he underlined the fact that I am underlining again, that the opposition were just repeating the same old accusations which had been answered. They seem to have heard and believed in the old saying of Voltaire: mentez, mentez, il en restera toujours quelque chose. They seem to think that if you repeat the same accusation often enough, people will remember only the accusation and forget the answer.
That is not a fair way to deal with the public of Canada. It is not a fair way to deal with the electors of this country. We all know that there are not so many people who read the reports of the committees. Nearly everyone reads what goes on in the house

The Address-Mr. Cannon
because it appears in the newspapers but only a comparative few read what goes on in the committees, so you have accusations being made in the house in a general way and then answered in detail in the committee. If those accusations are repeated often enough there is no doubt that they will be noticed more by the public and will eventually carry more weight than any answers that are given. I do not think that is a fair way to deal with this subject.
On this matter of so-called waste and extravagance, I was amazed to see that the items to which the opposition attached the most importance were things like neckties and shoes. I think we can consider we are lucky in this country when we realize that the government is spending $2,000 million on procurement, on armaments and things required for national defence, and the only criticism by the opposition has been in connection with things like neckties and shoes. We should consider ourselves lucky when we realize the enormous amounts that are spent on other items which are much more expensive and take up much more of the taxpayers' money.

I was very much interested to find in the Montreal Star of November 27 an extract from the good old London Times, which for once does not agree with the Leader of the Opposition. The article reads as follows:
The Times came out today with an analysis of the commonwealth economic conference that seems in complete accord with the Canadian viewpoint. In its leading editorial, the independent newspaper says the commonwealth ministers must have two main problems to consider: self-help within the sterling area and the fundamental problem of United States predominance.
The danger, says the Times, is that the second problem may be used by the sterling area as an excuse for not putting their own house in order. "Because of the persistent American surplus ... it is contended that the action now demanded to make the economies of the commonwealth countries shipshape ... is beside the mark", the newspaper adds. "In fact, the truth is precisely the opposite."
"The greater the difficulty of making both ends meet in world markets, the greater the need to leave nothing undone to make the most in competitive terms of commonwealth resources. The Times says it is clear, "as it has been all the time to the Canadians at their special vantage point in North America", that there is no solution in perpetual restriction.

I wish to draw the attention of the house to the fact that just one year ago now, in December 1951, we were all very much worried about the increase in the cost of living. Members of the opposition were all insisting that it was absolutely necessary, if we were going to avoid disastrous inflation and preserve the economy of our country, that controls be reimposed. The government held firm. Don't shake your head. The hon. member may not have advocated it, but there were members of the opposition who did. I remember very well. The government decided that it would not interfere directly with the liberties of the citizen and it would not impose controls, as it considered they were not necessary at the time. It decided to take indirect methods to control inflation. I am very gratified to say, Mr. Speaker, and I draw it to the attention of the opposition if they have not already noticed it, that the cost of living according to the old index has dropped from 191 in January of this year to 185 when last reported. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the whole cabinet deserve the congratulations of this house and of all fair-minded Canadians for their very wise attitude which has produced these results.

Mr. Speaker, with the house in the happy mood in which it is at the present moment, I am sure you and the house will not be disappointed if I make a speech on the subject of gold and the convertibility of currency. This matter is, and continues to be, one of the most important matters facing all the democratic countries. It is a subject which is under intense and vital discussion at the prime ministers' conference in London at the present time, so I feel that certain things should be said here concerning the problem.
I want to deal briefly with the new emergency gold mining regulations which were announced at the beginning of the session. The new formula continues the old type of assistance under the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act. Although it does increase slightly the payments to be made by the government, actually the new formula, like its predecessors, is of little real help. Many mines have worked out what this assistance will mean, and one of them-Bralome in British Columbia-has estimated that it will mean rather less than 50 cents an ounce. Actually I think it would be safe to say that the increase will not equal the increased cost of steel which has taken place in the past year. Certainly it will not equal the increase in the cost of steel and chemicals at any mine so far as I am aware. Nothing is done, of course, to overcome the problem of the wide labour differential between gold mines and the base metal mines which is causing so much trouble. I have heard it said that the increase will not compensate for the added cost of grinding balls and grinding rods in the grinding circuits of most mines.
I want to put the situation on this act as clearly as I can. The gold mines did not ask for a bonus. I have consistently said in this house that it was not right to ask the Canadian taxpayer to bonus any industry. Gold, like any other metal, should be sold for the price it can command, and any mine which cannot operate at that price should not be in operation. That price, however-this is the important factor-should be the free price and not the present broker-controlled price. There should be no restrictions on owning, storing, selling or exporting gold in any form. Only in this manner can we arrive at a true price. The $14 million we are currently asking from the taxpayer is an unnecessary burden. Furthermore, it is doing the mines no real good. Unfortunately the industry has now come to depend on this assistance, and it will probably be impossible to cut it off until the free market is well

Let us look at this business of the free market. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has repeatedly stated in this house that the United States controls the price of gold. Actually, Mr. Speaker, nothing could be further from the truth. The United States, because of the restrictions it imposes on the ownership of gold and which are similar to ours, can under no circumstances be considered as being on the gold standard. Unless the treasury or the central bank will sell gold freely to its citizens and give gold in exchange for currency to any citizen requiring it, a country cannot be said to have a fully exchangeable gold standard. As I say, today the United States does not control the price of gold. If the United States stopped buying gold altogether it would not injure the Canadian gold mining industry. Actually, I believe it would help it.

the past I have disagreed with the international monetary fund, and still disagree as to their policies, nevertheless we must believe that their statistics are correct.
We now come to the point that gold is what used to be called in my school days the X factor in the simultaneous equation; in other words, that gold is the common denominator upon which all currencies are equated. We have today the principal problem of trade between the commonwealth and the sterling area and ourselves in the dollar bloc. There is the fiction that there is a shortage of dollars. The United Kingdom continues to talk about a shortage of dollars; all the sterling bloc talks about a shortage of dollars. What they mean is that they have a shortage of goods to sell for gold. How are you going to get those United States dollars if the United States will only accept dollars or gold?
The way to do that is to bring gold out in the open so that the owners of any currencies, the owners of any goods, may be paid for in the open in terms of gold, which has a purchasing power all over the world. I do not say this will cure the difficulty, but it is one of the steps which should be taken so that the impasse between the sterling bloc and the dollar bloc can be broken down and have a common denominator in the market places of the world in terms of the one thing that all currencies are equated in, namely gold. It is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that we have lost the opportunity of our young nationhood in not having gone ahead with this market long before this.
I come now to the United Kingdom problems. Twice in my lifetime has the freedom of the world been saved by the heroic actions of the citizens of that small island. It may well be that the wise counsel prevailing in London will be able to bridge the impasse that now exists in the United Nations. No man who is free today can ever pay his debt to the United Kingdom. But, Mr. Speaker, so long as wrong economics guide the policies, there is nothing very much that can be done. So long as currency control, embargoes and restrictions are imposed by any country, that country cannot go ahead and prosper the way it should, irrespective of the efforts of its people, great as they are.
There is of course the question in this case of the sterling balances to Egypt and the sterling balances to India. I feel that just as the war debts were found impossible of payment after the first world war, so the sterling debts which the United Kingdom accepted so readily to preserve the very freedom of both India and Egypt, and many other countries, should be treated very largely in

the same way as the debts to the United States of the first world war. To pay them is like borrowing a man's garden hose to put out a fire in his house, and then having him charge you for the water you used to put out the fire.
That, however, is a problem which overhangs the whole question of convertibility, and I shall not go into details in a speech in this house. Convertibility is one thing. Convertibility can be assisted by a free market in the common denominator of all currencies, namely gold. But besides convertibility we must have trade. As a matter of fact the two go hand in hand. Today there is fortunately a very distinct change coming over United States thinking in this regard.
I should like to mention the opinions of Dr. Benjamin Beckhart, who is the economic consultant of the Chase national bank. He is also professor of banking of the Columbia graduate school of business. Dr. Beckhart is an economist of note. But it is not because of his ability as an economist that I am quoting his opinions at the moment. It is because what he says is significant of the new trend in American thought. Dr. Beckhart said that in order to overcome this question of convertibility and trade, certain things had to be done. He suggested that the United States should lend assistance to Great Britain and other European countries who were trying to return to currency convertibility to take steps so that raids on their currencies would be prevented. He suggested that the international monetary fund should grant stand-by drawing accounts.
Another very important proposal was that there should be repeal of the buy-American acts, an extension of the reciprocal trade agreement acts, an effort to delete the peril point clause and the escape clauses. He said also that there should be a rewriting of the customs law so that it might be greatly simplified.
This gentleman is representative of the very highest type of modern American business. He is, if I may say so, representative of the sort of thought that is going into the future Republican administration in the United States. I believe it shows a very significant and hopeful change in the American attitude when we see men of Dr. Beckhart's calibre making these suggestions.

It is still with us; and because in the last year we had a slight falling-off in the cost of living we would be foolish to believe that there has been a reversal of the trend. What happens if this goes on? It simply means that the value of the dollar decreases just that much every year. If this trend goes on it means that in respect of things such as old age pensions, a man now in his fifties who is paying for an old age pension will, at the age of seventy, draw in terms of today's dollar, a sum equal to about $19. This must be stopped; because if it is not stopped we will destroy the very security we are trying to protect. Someone may say that it is all very well, that a man can invest in common stock equities, that a man can invest in prime real estate or buy a farm or take his money out of the country. That is all very well for the wealthy. But today in Montreal and Toronto only 6 per cent of all wage earners earn more than $4,000 a year. .Recent surveys show that 94 per cent of all the wage earners in Montreal and Toronto receive $4,000 a year or less and must depend upon such things as life insurance, government bonds and bank savings accounts. It is their security that we are destroying by this constant inflation.	.
From time to time I have suggested that the only way to attack inflation, the only way to stop this rot in the currency, is by returning to a fixed gold standard. That is some distance in the future; it is not practical immediately because we do not know what the price of gold is going to be. We do not know where it will stabilize itself. But we do see the rot, we do see this thing going on and we are as yet powerless to stop it.
Because there has been a decrease in the cost of living during the last six or eight months can we say that is the trend, especially with an increased cost for basic steel, and increased cost for coal and undoubtedly an added cost for freight because of higher wage rates for the railway workers? To do so I think would be unwise and wrong in every possible way. We say that we are having a boom. Our trade is at record levels. We are spending $500 million at Kitimat; we are building the St. Lawrence power project and waterway by ourselves. Our dollar is at a premium. Our budget is in balance, with a huge surplus. Those are fine things, of which every Canadian should be proud; but what good are they if the security of the people we are trying to protect is destroyed? This is not happening quickly as was the case with inflation in Germany, but there is a continual eating away of the purchasing power of our currency, and with it goes the savings of our people.
To say that the trend is downward and inflation beaten because a few indices have turned downward, is it not rather like saying that highway fatalities have stopped, that we have cured the highway traffic accident problem because there has been a week end without fatality or a Christmas season practically free from accidents? I think both arguments would be completely fallacious.


I should like to say one word about the price of gold. It is not the function of any government to set the price of gold. Gold is not the plaything of any political party. Gold is the people's security against all political parties. Until the people are allowed to have gold, that security is taken away from them by this inflation I have been talking about.
I do not know what it will be set at. I have no idea where it will adjust itself. But if it follows the general line and if the price before the war was adequate, we must think of gold in terms of the indices which I have quoted and expect a price at least double, or probably more, the pre-war price before it can properly fulfil its function. To place gold at any price and not let it go free would be just as dangerous and wrong as to maintain it at its present price and thus destroy the mining industry. The prime function of gold is to act as a monetary value. To sterilize it even at any price and not allow it to fulfil its historical function of being the safeguard of the savings of the people is wrong and dangerous. Furthermore it is the road to revolution.

Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess I was trying to make one point, namely that no government has the right or prerogative to say what the price of gold shall be unless that government is prepared to exchange the national currency into gold at that rate without restrictions of any sort whatsoever. I think the incoming administration at Washington understands that. Gold is the citizen's supreme safeguard against dishonest government.
I want to refer briefly now to the possible -I do not say "proposed" although it is proposed-diversion of water from the Atlin lakes in British Columbia and the Yukon and also from lake Laberge over the pass down to Skagway, Alaska, for the development of a very large amount of hydroelectric energy and the creation of an aluminum smelter. There are certain factors to be considered. The Yukon needs power to develop her natural resources and the promise of this abundant electric power is certainly very tempting. However, the water belongs to the province of British Columbia which under

the British North America Act is the owner of her own natural resources, and her interests must certainly be considered. If I were a British Columbian, particularly one from the northern part of the province, I would give the matter most serious thought before I approved of the removal from the province of so much essential primary power.
The next point is that the future of the Yukon lies in the development of her mineral resources. There are two essential requirements involved. One is power and the other is water as distinct from power. The new discoveries of potentially great mineral resources that have been indicated by companies such as Hudson Bay, Ventures and others will certainly require power, but they will also require water. They will require water for their milling and mining and for the use of the communities that may grow up around these developments if they take place. The potential of the Yukon is just being remotely scratched at the present time.
In the last few months the indications have been that there is a storehouse of minerals there equal to or greater than that of old Ontario and Quebec. We speak of "old Ontario" now as being the Timmins and Kirkland Lake area and of "old Quebec" as being the Noranda and Bourlamaque belt.
If the storehouse of the Yukon is to be developed we will require power; but we will also require water, and if the Yukon river is diverted to such a degree that this essential water is taken from us it may seriously hinder the development of these new mining properties. I realize it is more efficient from the point of view of per cubic foot of water to turn it over the pass and get a thousand foot head instead of taking it down the Yukon river. Infinitely more power can be developed in this way than at such sites as Miles canyon and others on the river; but the essential thing is that we must take great care not to lose the water without adequate safeguard.
The question of navigation also is important. The Yukon river is shallow, and the removal of a large percentage of the flow of water from the lakes and headwaters feeding the Yukon river will make navigation that much more difficult. There is some coal development at Carmacks but it is not of a very high quality and the obtaining of power therefrom is certainly a doubtful economic factor. The Yukon river freezes five or six feet deep, but there is still water flowing underneath it at Dawson. If the flow is considerably decreased it is conceivable that the Yukon may freeze solid, as do such rivers as the Hay, and become useless in wintertime as a source of water.
